title: Penny Hardaway Sees Himself and Iverson in SGA
htmlContent:
When Brandon "Scoop B" Robinson sits down with a basketball legend, the conversation rarely stays in one decade. His latest #WORDWITHSCOOP exchange with Anfernee "Penny" Hardaway proved the point, moving from the arena sound systems of 1990s Orlando to the free-agency chess matches of today and, finally, to one of the hardest guards to stop in the modern NBA.

Scoop B has been at this a long time. He was covering the Nets as a 12-year-old in the late 1990s, co-hosting a team show while most kids his age were still collecting trading cards. That history gives his interviews a particular texture: he asks questions as a reporter, but also as someone who watched these players in real time and remembers the details.

Few interviewers would think to ask Penny whether the George Clinton track pumping through the Orlando arena ever tempted him to dance while bringing the ball up the floor. Penny's answer was as smooth as his crossover. No, he had the basketball, and the dancing was better left to Shaqand Dennis Scott.

Then the conversation turned. Scoop B asked which modern player move echoes Shaquille O'Neal leaving Orlando for the Lakers. Penny admitted he had never been asked that before, which says something about the freshness of the question. He pointed to Giannis Antetokounmpo chasing a title in Miami as the big-man parallel, and for a guard who leaves to chase something new, he named Ja Morant, a fitting choice for a coach who has spent years building his program in Memphis.

The legacy question came next: who did Penny influence more, LeBron James or Tracy McGrady? He chose McGrady. T-Mac grew up in Florida watching Penny run the Magic, and he wore No. 1 in his honor.LeBron respects his game, Penny said, but the line from Orlando to McGrady is direct.

All of that set the table for the question that gave the interview its spark. Scoop B offered a theory: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander reminds him of Penny because of his height, but SGA's shiftiness makes him look like a hybrid of Penny and Allen Iverson.

It is a sharp observation. At his peak, Penny was the prototype for the oversized point guard, a 6-foot-7 playmaker who could see over defenses and glide past them. Iverson was the opposite build with a similar effect: a smaller, relentless scorer who used hesitations and sudden bursts to create space nobody else could find. Gilgeous-Alexander, the Oklahoma City Thunder star, blends both. He has the length to rise over defenders and the herky-jerky rhythm that leaves them leaning the wrong way.

Penny didn't just agree; he built on the idea. He said he sees greatness in SGA's game, pointing to "the speed bursts, the change of speed and getting to his spots." He noted how Gilgeous-Alexander can shoot over opponents or go around them, and how he delivers in big moments, a trait Penny tied directly to Iverson.

"That's a pretty dope mix right there." —Penny Hardaway

What makes the exchange work is the way Scoop B framed it. Instead of asking Penny to rank SGA or argue an MVP case, he handed Penny a lens built from Penny's own career and invited him to look through it. The result was an answer that felt like scouting from someone who knows the position from the inside. Penny wasn't describing statistics; he was describing feel, the pace changes and favorite spots that only a fellow playmaker notices.

The comparison also reframes how fans might think about Penny's legacy. Injuries shortened his prime, and he never won a ring, but his blueprint shows up all over today's positionless NBA. Tall guards who handle, pass and score from all three levels are now common. When Penny looks at Gilgeous-Alexander, he is seeing a version of the future he helped sketch out in the 1990s, upgraded with an Iverson-style bag of tricks.

That is the value of a good interviewer. Scoop B didn't just collect quotes. He connected eras, and in doing so gave one of the game's great stylists a chance to recognize his own influence in the league's present.
excerpt: In a wide-ranging #WORDWITHSCOOP interview with Brandon "Scoop B" Robinson, Penny Hardaway praised Shai Gilgeous-Alexander as a "pretty dope mix" of himself and Allen Iverson, citing SGA's length, speed bursts, change of pace, and clutch scoring ability.
